content: Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a specific disease that occur within a defined time period, typically one year. It can be expressed either as a proportion or as a rate. The incidence proportion, also referred to as risk, is calculated by dividing the number of new cases by the size of the population at risk. For instance, in a stable population of 1,000 individuals, if 28 people develop a condition over a two-year observation period, the incidence proportion would be 28 cases per 1,000 individuals. The incidence rate, on the other hand, is determined by the number of new cases per unit of person-time at risk. Using the same example, the incidence rate would be 14 cases per 1,000 person-years. This is calculated by dividing the incidence proportion (28 per 1,000) by the duration of observation (two years). The use of person-time accounts for situations where some individuals may leave the study before its completion. It is important to note that the term incidence is sometimes used informally to refer to the incidence rate, though this is not precise terminology. Incidence should not be confused with prevalence. In other words, incidence provides information about the risk of developing the disease, while prevalence indicates how widespread the disease is within the population. For example, consider a disease that was widely spread in 2002 but whose transmission was halted in 2003. If the disease takes a long time to cure, it would have both a high prevalence and a high incidence in 2002. However, in 2003, the incidence would be low because new cases are no longer occurring, but the prevalence would remain high due to the prolonged duration of the disease. Conversely, a disease with a short duration may exhibit a high incidence but a low prevalence, as cases resolve quickly.
